questions.question: A language model reads text as tokens: pieces such as words or parts of words. Byte-pair encoding builds the list of tokens from a text, one step at a time. What does one step do?

options.text: It adds every word of the text to the list at once, one token per word
options.why: Whole words are never added directly. Tokens grow from single bytes by joining pairs, so a common word may become one token while a rare one stays in pieces.

options.text: It joins the rarest pair of neighbours first, so that unusual words get tokens of their own
options.why: The most frequent pair is joined first. That is what shortens the text most.

options.text: It joins the most frequent pair of neighbouring pieces into one new token
options.why: It counts every pair of neighbouring pieces in the text and joins the most frequent pair everywhere it occurs. Each step adds exactly one token. The list of joins, in order, is all the cutting rule learns.

options.text: It gives each letter a number and stops there
options.why: That is only the starting alphabet: the 256 possible byte values, the numbers a computer stores text with. The joins build longer tokens on top of it.

questions.question: A token's id can be written as a list as long as the vocabulary: a 1 at the token's place and 0 everywhere else. This is called a one-hot vector. Why does it say which token it is and nothing more?

options.text: Any two such lists are the same distance apart, so no token is nearer another
options.why: Two different one-hot lists differ in exactly two places, so every pair is the same distance apart, the square root of 2. With all distances equal, no relation between tokens can show.

options.text: Its single 1 is put at a random place
options.why: The 1 sits at the place given by the token's id. It is fixed, not random.

options.text: A larger id puts the 1 further along, so later tokens count as larger
options.why: The place of the 1 is only a label. Token 271 is not more than token 40 in any sense.

options.text: It stores the letters of the token, so tokens that share letters sit closer
options.why: It stores only which id the token has. The letters inside a token are never represented separately.

questions.question: In a model, each token of a sentence is a list of numbers, and the lists are mixed by averaging them with weights. The sentence and the same words shuffled give the same result. What makes the word order count?

options.text: Mixing more times, so that later rounds can see the order
options.why: Every round that treats positions alike is as blind as the first. More rounds do not supply order.

options.text: Adding a list that stands for the position to each token's list before mixing
options.why: With a position added, the same token at two positions becomes two different lists. The mixing weights then differ, and the two sentences no longer give the same result.

options.text: Training the token lists for longer, until each learns where its token stands
options.why: A token's list depends on its id alone, not on where it stands. No amount of training puts the position into it.

options.text: Taking the average of the lists instead of their sum
options.why: An average is as blind to order as a sum. Both give the same result for the sentence and its shuffle.

questions.question: Computers store text as bytes, numbers from 0 to 255. Each character has a code point, its number in the Unicode table; code points below 128 take one byte, those up to 2047 take two. The word café is typed as c, a, f, e and then the combining accent U+0301 (code point 769). How many characters, code points and bytes is that?

options.text: 4 characters, 4 code points, 5 bytes
options.why: That is the other spelling, with é as the single code point U+00E9. The spelling here has a fifth code point for the accent.

options.text: 5 characters, 5 code points and 5 bytes
options.why: The eye sees four characters, not five: the accent sits on the e. And the accent needs two bytes, since its code point is above 127.

options.text: 4 characters, 5 code points, 5 bytes
options.why: Only code points below 128 fit in one byte. 769 needs two.

options.text: 4 characters, 5 code points, 6 bytes
options.why: The letters c, a, f and e take one byte each. The accent's code point, 769, is below 2048, so it takes two bytes: 4 + 2 = 6.

questions.question: A vocabulary starts from the 256 byte values and grows by one token per join. It has had 150 joins. The next join merges a pair that occurs 40 times in a text of 600 tokens. What are the vocabulary size and the text length after it?

options.text: 407 tokens in the vocabulary and 560 in the text
options.why: The vocabulary is 256 plus the number of joins: 256 + 151 = 407. Each occurrence of the pair turns two tokens into one, which removes 40 tokens: 600 - 40 = 560.

options.text: 407 tokens in the vocabulary and 520 tokens in the text
options.why: Each join removes one token, not two: two pieces become one.

options.text: 296 tokens in the vocabulary and 560 in the text
options.why: A join adds one token however often the pair occurs. 296 counts a new token for every occurrence.

options.text: 406 tokens in the vocabulary and 560 in the text
options.why: 406 is 256 + 150, the size before this join. The new join adds one more.

questions.question: Inside a model, attention gives every pair of tokens a score, so a text of n tokens needs n times n scores. A sentence is 30 tokens in English and 75 tokens in a script the vocabulary never saw. How many times larger is the table of scores for the second?

options.text: 2.5 times
options.why: 2.5 is the ratio of the token counts. The table grows with the square of the count.

options.text: 15.6 times
options.why: 15.6 is 2.5 cubed. One score per pair of tokens makes a square, not a cube.

options.text: 6.25 times: 5625 scores against 900
options.why: The table has one score per pair of tokens, n squared. 75 x 75 = 5625 and 30 x 30 = 900, and 5625 / 900 = 6.25.

options.text: The same size, since the meaning is the same
options.why: Cost is counted in tokens, not in meaning. The same sentence in more tokens costs more.

questions.question: A model gives each possible next token a score, and the scores are turned into probabilities: each score s becomes e to the power s, divided by the total. A temperature divides every score before this. Three tokens have scores 2, 1 and 0, and the top token gets about 0.665. What does it get at temperature 0.5?

options.text: About 0.506
options.why: 0.506 is the result at temperature 2. Above 1 the shares even out; below 1 they sharpen.

options.text: Still 0.665, since every score is divided by the same number
options.why: Dividing scores is not dividing probabilities. Through the power of e, it changes the gaps between them.

options.text: Exactly 1, since below 1 only the top token is kept
options.why: Only a temperature at zero leaves a single token. At 0.5 the other two tokens still hold about 13 per cent together.

options.text: About 0.867
options.why: Dividing by 0.5 gives scores 4, 2 and 0, and e^4 / (e^4 + e^2 + e^0) is about 0.867. A temperature below 1 makes the likeliest token likelier.

questions.question: Why can one extra space at the start of a request change a language model's answer?

options.text: The model treats spaces as instructions about how to answer
options.why: Nothing tells the model anything about spaces. The change comes from how the text is cut into tokens, before the model runs.

options.text: The space joins the first word's token, so that word gets another id
options.why: 'the' with a space in front and 'the' without are different tokens with different ids. The first word therefore gets a different list of numbers, and everything after is computed from the lists that went in.

options.text: Spaces are removed before the model sees the text, but the token count changes
options.why: Spaces are not removed. Each is glued to the word after it, and that is the cause.

options.text: The space pushes the last token of the request out of what the model can read
options.why: One extra token hardly matters when the model reads many tokens at once. The changed id of the first word matters far more.

questions.question: To compare two passages, a model's lists of numbers, one per token, are averaged into one list per passage. Two passages share almost all their words, but one has a single 'not' and means the opposite. Their lists come out close. Why?

options.text: The model has judged that the two passages mean the same, despite the 'not'
options.why: The model was never asked about meaning. The closeness is a property of the averaging, not a judgement.

options.text: The comparison ignores negative numbers
options.why: The comparison uses every number, positive or negative. The issue is how little one word changes the average.

options.text: One averaged list sums up the words used, and one 'not' barely moves it
options.why: The average runs over many positions, and a single word is one of them. Collapsing a passage to one list loses detail. Passages that share words and structure sit close whatever they say.

options.text: The lists are too short to hold a 'not' alongside the other words
options.why: Length is not the limit. One position carries 'not' without trouble; the average dilutes it among all the others.

questions.question: A model is trained on whole texts at once, yet it writes one token at a time, never seeing what comes after. Why do the two match?

options.text: In training, a mask hides the later tokens, which writing never has
options.why: Each training guess uses only earlier tokens: the scores for later tokens are set to minus infinity, so no token reads ahead. When writing, there is nothing ahead to read, so the situation is the same.

options.text: The model memorises every training text and replays it one token at a time
options.why: A small model trained on one text does lean on it, but the match comes from the mask, not from memory.

options.text: The store of keys and values keeps the training texts
options.why: That store keeps numbers computed for the earlier tokens of the current text, to save work. It does not make training and writing agree.

options.text: Writing also looks ahead at the tokens to come, as training does
options.why: The tokens ahead do not exist yet while writing. That is why training must be blind to them too.
